section.title: Day of Disaster, Trust, and the Sabbath
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah is forbidden even ordinary human joys, marriage, mourning, feasting, as a living sign of the total disaster coming on Judah, yet within that same darkness God promises a future so great it will eclipse the exodus itself. The passage then turns to timeless wisdom: the heart is deceitful above all things, blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD like a tree planted by the waters, and finally a call to keep the Sabbath holy as a test of covenant loyalty.
section.thesis: Judah's judgment is so total that even the prophet's private life becomes a sign of it, yet God's ultimate word is not despair: cursed is the one who trusts in man, blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD, and even now, keeping the Sabbath holy remains the open door to renewed blessing for a people whose only hope is the LORD who searches the heart and rewards according to true faithfulness.
section.frameNote: Six movements: Jeremiah's own forbidden marriage, mourning, and feasting as a sign of total judgment; the promise of a future deliverance greater than the exodus; sin engraved on the heart and judgment on the high places; the contrast between the cursed one who trusts in man and the blessed one who trusts in the LORD, like a tree planted by the waters; Jeremiah's own plea for healing and vindication before his persecutors; and the call to keep the Sabbath day holy as the test of covenant loyalty at Jerusalem's gates.

units.label: You must not marry
units.note: a sign act of total judgment

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place.”
For this is what the LORD says concerning the sons and daughters born in this place, and the mothers who bore them, and the fathers who fathered them in this land:

“They will die from deadly diseases. They will not be mourned or buried, but will lie like dung on the ground. They will be finished off by sword and famine, and their corpses will become food for the birds of the air and beasts of the earth.”

Indeed, this is what the LORD says: “Do not enter a house where there is a funeral meal. Do not go to {{ebel|mourn}} or show sympathy, for I have removed from this people My peace, My loving devotion, and My compassion,” declares the LORD.
“Both great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried or mourned, nor will anyone cut himself or shave his head for them.
No food will be offered to comfort those who mourn the dead; not even a cup of consolation will be given for the loss of a father or mother.
You must not enter a house where there is feasting and sit down with them to eat and drink.

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am going to remove from this place, before your very eyes and in your days, the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom.

When you tell these people all these things, they will ask you, ‘Why has the LORD pronounced all this great disaster against us? What is our guilt? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?’

Then you are to answer them: ‘It is because your fathers have forsaken Me, declares the LORD, and followed other gods, and served and worshiped them. They abandoned Me and did not keep My instruction.
And you have done more evil than your fathers. See how each of you follows the stubbornness of his evil heart instead of obeying Me.
So I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known. There you will serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.’

units.label: As surely as the LORD lives
units.note: a hope greater than the exodus

verses.text: Yet behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they will no longer say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.’

Instead they will say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.’ For I will return them to their land that I gave to their forefathers.

But for now I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them. After that I will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them down on every mountain and hill, even from the clefts of the rocks.
For My eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from My face, and their guilt is not concealed from My eyes.

And I will first repay them double their iniquity and their sin, because they have defiled My land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and they have filled My inheritance with their abominations.”

O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress, the nations will come to You from the ends of the earth, and they will say, “Our fathers inherited nothing but lies, worthless idols of no benefit at all.
Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods!”

“Therefore behold, I will inform them, and this time I will make them know 
My power and My might; then they will know that My name is the LORD.

units.label: The sin of Judah is written
units.note: engraved sin and judgment on the high places

verses.text: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars.
Even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills.

O My mountain in the countryside, I will give over your wealth 
and all your treasures as plunder, because of the sin of your high places, within all your borders.
And you yourself will relinquish the inheritance that I gave you. I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know, for you have kindled My anger; it will burn forever.”

units.label: Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind
units.note: a tree planted by the waters

verses.text:
This is what the LORD says: 
“Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes the flesh his strength 
and turns his heart from the LORD.
He will be like a shrub in the desert; he will not see when prosperity comes. He will dwell in the parched places of the desert, in a salt land where no one lives.
But blessed is the man who {{batach|trusts}} in the LORD, whose confidence is in Him.

He is like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream. It does not fear when the heat comes, and its leaves are always green. It does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit.

The {{lev|heart}} is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. 
Who can understand it?
I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve.
Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly. In the middle of his days his riches will desert him, and in the end he will be the fool.”
A glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary.

O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who abandon You will be put to shame. All who turn away will be written in the dust, for they have abandoned the LORD, 
the fountain of living water.

Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, 
for You are my praise.

Behold, they keep saying to me, “Where is the word of the LORD? 
Let it come now!”
But I have not run away from being Your shepherd; I have not desired the day of despair. You know that the utterance of my lips was spoken in Your presence.
Do not become a terror to me; You are my refuge in the day of disaster.

Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame. Let them be terrified, but do not let me be terrified. Bring upon them the day of disaster and shatter them with double destruction.

units.label: Keep the Sabbath day holy
units.note: the test of covenant loyalty at the gates

verses.text: This is what the LORD said to me: “Go and stand at the gate of the people, through which the kings of Judah go in and out; and stand at all the other gates of Jerusalem.
Say to them, ‘Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, all people of Judah and Jerusalem who enter through these gates.
This is what the LORD says: Take heed for yourselves; do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day.
You must not carry a load out of your houses or do any work on the {{shabbat|Sabbath}} day, but you must keep the Sabbath day holy, just as I commanded your forefathers.
Yet they would not listen or incline their ear, but they stiffened their necks and would not listen or receive My discipline.
If, however, you listen carefully to Me, says the LORD, and bring no load through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, and keep the Sabbath day holy, and do no work on it,

then kings and princes will enter through the gates of this city. They will sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses with their officials, along with the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever.

And people will come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, and from the foothills, the hill country, and the Negev, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and thank offerings to the house of the LORD.

But if you do not listen to Me to keep the Sabbath day holy by not carrying a load while entering the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle an unquenchable fire in its gates to consume the citadels of Jerusalem.’”

ebel.gloss: Mourning, grief expressed in formal customs. Jeremiah is forbidden even to mourn the dead, since the coming devastation will be too vast and too constant for ordinary grieving customs to keep pace with it.

batach.gloss: To trust, to feel secure or confident in someone or something. The chapter contrasts trusting in mere flesh, which withers like a desert shrub, with trusting in the LORD, which flourishes like a tree planted by the waters.

lev.gloss: The heart, seat of will, thought, and desire in Hebrew thought. Jeremiah declares the heart deceitful above all things, beyond human cure, showing that any hope for change must come from outside the self, ultimately fulfilled in the new heart promised later in this book.

shabbat.gloss: Sabbath, the seventh day set apart for rest, commanded from creation and reaffirmed at Sinai. Keeping it holy becomes, at Jerusalem's very gates, the visible test of whether the nation will listen to the LORD at all.

basic.context: God forbids Jeremiah even the ordinary comforts of life, marriage, mourning the dead, feasting with neighbors, each becoming a living sign act of the totality of coming judgment: no families will be left to marry, no mourners to grieve, no joy to celebrate. Yet in the middle of this bleak sign, God promises a future deliverance so great that people will no longer swear by the exodus from Egypt but by this new gathering from every land. The passage then turns from Jeremiah's own life to timeless wisdom about the human heart and the choice between trusting in man and trusting in the LORD, before closing with a call to keep the Sabbath holy as the visible mark of covenant loyalty.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage mixes a dramatic personal sign act, oracles of both severe judgment and startling future hope, wisdom sayings resembling the Psalms, and covenant instruction about the Sabbath, showing how varied the prophetic voice can be within a single unit. The famous contrast between the cursed man who trusts in flesh and the blessed man like a tree planted by the waters closely parallels Psalm 1, suggesting a shared wisdom tradition applied here to a specific national crisis.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah is told not even to ebel, mourn, for the dead, since mourning itself will become pointless amid such devastation. Blessed is the one who batach, trusts, in the LORD, in contrast to the one who trusts in mere flesh; yet the human lev, heart, is deceitful above all things, so trust must be placed outside the self, in God alone. Finally, keeping the shabbat, Sabbath, holy becomes the visible sign of whether Judah will listen to the LORD at all.
basic.typology: The forbidden mourning, marriage, and feasting given to Jeremiah, meant to embody Judah's coming devastation, points forward by contrast to Christ, who both mourns, Luke 19:41, and provides a wedding feast that will never be interrupted, Revelation 19:9. The tree planted by the waters, never withering, anticipates the fruitfulness promised to those who abide in Christ, John 15:5.
basic.christ: The blessed man who trusts in the LORD, like a tree planted by the waters whose leaves are always green, finds its fullest picture in those who abide in Christ, the true vine, bearing fruit that does not wither, John 15:1-5. And where Jeremiah confesses that the heart is deceitful above all things, the gospel answers with the promise of a new heart and a new covenant written within, later unfolded in Jeremiah 31:33 and fulfilled through the Spirit poured out at Pentecost.
basic.god: God's judgment here is total enough to touch even the ordinary rhythms of marriage, mourning, and feasting, yet He is also the God who searches the heart and tests the mind to reward each according to his deeds, showing His judgment is never careless but perfectly discerning. His call to keep the Sabbath holy at the very gates of Jerusalem shows that even at this late hour, covenant blessing remains genuinely open to a people willing to listen.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 1 offers a close parallel to the tree planted by streams of water. Jeremiah 31:33 promises the new heart and new covenant that answers the deceitful heart named here. John 15:1-5 pictures believers abiding in Christ the vine, bearing fruit that does not wither. Revelation 19:9 promises the wedding feast of the Lamb that will never be interrupted.
basic.oneStory: This is the sober picture of judgment so complete it silences even ordinary human joy, set beside the timeless call to trust the LORD rather than mere flesh, a call answered fully in Christ, the true vine in whom those who abide bear fruit that never withers, and in whom the promised new heart, replacing the deceitful one exposed here, is finally given.

context.literary:
The unit is a mosaic held together by two threads, the heart and the gates. It opens with three prohibitions, 16:1 to 9: no wife and children, no entering a house of mourning, no entering a house of feasting. Each carries its own reason, and the three together strip away the three great occasions of village life, a birth, a funeral and a feast. Verses 10 to 13 then stage a question and answer that anticipates the people's protest, 'What is our guilt?', and gives the reply in advance. Verses 14 and 15 break in with 'Yet behold, the days are coming,' a promise of return that reappears almost word for word in 23:7 and 8. Verses 16 to 18 return to judgment with the images of fishermen and hunters, and 16:19 to 21 is a startling prayer in which the nations come from the ends of the earth confessing that their fathers' idols were lies.

Chapter 17 begins with sin engraved on hearts and altars, then pairs the cursed man and the blessed man, 17:5 to 8, a poem built as a mirror: shrub in the desert against tree by the water. The heart appears in 17:1, 5, 9 and 10, so the poem is not a stray piece of wisdom but the centre of the argument: the issue is where the heart is anchored. After a proverb about the partridge, 17:11, a short hymn to the temple throne, 17:12 and 13, leads into the prophet's fourth confession, 17:14 to 18. The unit ends with the Sabbath sermon at the gates, 17:19 to 27.

The two bookends answer each other. The opening denies Jeremiah the ordinary rhythms of life; the closing offers Judah an ordinary day, the Sabbath, as the test of whether she will live. The 'gates' of the closing sermon recur like a drumbeat, in the courtyard where kings enter and leave, and the passage ends with fire in those same gates.
context.historical:
Jeremiah's three prohibitions would have been felt in a society where marriage and burial were obligations of kin. A funeral meal, the marzeach of 16:5, was a communal gathering that comforted survivors, and the same word appears in Amos 6:7 for a feasting society. Cutting the body and shaving the head for the dead, 16:6, were mourning customs that the law had forbidden, Leviticus 19:28 and Deuteronomy 14:1, yet they were evidently practised, which is why Jeremiah can mention them as a matter of course. The nearest parallel to the sign is Ezekiel's, who was told not to mourn when his wife died, Ezekiel 24:15 to 24. In both cases the prophet's refusal to grieve is meant to teach the people that the disaster to come will be too large for the rites.

The time is probably the reign of Jehoiakim, 609 to 598 BC, though the text does not say. The altars with Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills, 17:2, belong to the long history of local cults that Josiah's reform had tried to remove. The 'horns of their altars,' 17:1, were the projections at the corners where the blood of the sin offering was put, Leviticus 4:25. The picture is that the very place where sin was cleansed now has sin engraved on it.

The Sabbath sermon assumes that goods were carried through Jerusalem's gates on the seventh day. Nehemiah met the same trade at the gates a century and a half later and shut them, Nehemiah 13:15 to 19, and reminded the nobles of this history, Nehemiah 13:18. The Sabbath was not a private habit but a public sign of the covenant, Exodus 31:13, and a city that traded on the day showed whose it thought it was.
context.canonical:
The cursed and blessed man of 17:5 to 8 is a sibling of Psalm 1, where the blessed man is like a tree planted by streams of water, Psalm 1:3. Jeremiah uses the covenant words for cursed and blessed, as in Deuteronomy 27 and 28, rather than the psalm's 'happy,' so he makes the choice a covenant sanction. Psalm 92:12 to 14 adds the picture of the righteous flourishing in old age.

The deceitful heart reaches back to Genesis, where the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth, Genesis 8:21. Jeremiah's answer to it is stated in his own book: a new covenant in which God writes His law on the heart, 31:33, and gives a heart to know Him, 24:7. Ezekiel promises a new heart in place of the heart of stone, Ezekiel 36:26, and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's promise as fulfilled in Christ, Hebrews 8:10. Paul describes the church as a letter written 'not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3, which is an answer to the iron stylus of 17:1.

The bridegroom's voice that is silenced in 16:9 is silenced again in 7:34 and 25:10 and promised back in 33:10 and 11. In Revelation it falls silent in Babylon, 18:23, and sounds at the marriage supper of the Lamb, 19:9. The fountain of living water of 17:13 is Jesus' gift to the thirsty, John 4:10 and 7:37 and 38. The Sabbath of 17:19 to 27 is taken up in Jesus' lordship over the Sabbath, Matthew 12:8, and in the rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The text wants Judah to hear four things. First, that the coming catastrophe is not random: the question 'Why?' of 16:10 is answered, and the answer is the long record of other gods and a present generation that outdid its fathers. Second, that there is a future beyond the judgment, and that it will be so great that Israel will re-tell its founding story. Verses 14 and 15 are not a footnote of comfort but a claim that God's power to rescue will be shown more fully than at the Red Sea.

Third, that the problem is not merely external practice. 17:1 to 10 turns attention inward, to the heart where idolatry begins, and declares that human beings cannot solve this by self-knowledge, since the heart is beyond their understanding. Only the LORD who searches it can judge it, and trust must therefore be placed in Him.

Fourth, that the Sabbath was a doorway to life. The sermon in 17:19 to 27 does not treat the day as a rule for its own sake. It is offered as the one concrete act by which the city could reverse its fate, with a promise of kings on David's throne and worshipers from every region if they obey, and unquenchable fire if they do not. Jeremiah, forbidden every ordinary comfort, is being asked by God to speak to the city about an ordinary day.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The three prohibitions of 16:1 to 9 are a sign for Jeremiah in his particular office, not a command for the people of God. They do not teach that believers should avoid weddings, funerals or celebrations. Jesus wept at a grave, John 11:35, and says that those who mourn are blessed, Matthew 5:4. The point is that for this prophet at this hour, the usual rites would have been a lie.

The line that the heart is deceitful above all things describes the human condition under sin, and Jeremiah supplies the remedy elsewhere in the book. It is not licence to distrust every feeling or an invitation to endless introspection, but a warning against relying on oneself, 17:5.

The Sabbath instruction is addressed to Judah in covenant with the LORD, and its terms are specific: no loads through Jerusalem's gates. The principle that carries over is that God's people rest, and that rest is an act of trust. How this is lived now is argued among Christians, and the New Testament speaks of a rest that remains, Hebrews 4:9, and of Jesus as Lord of the Sabbath, Mark 2:27 and Matthew 12:8. Whatever else is said, the text cannot be used to say that the day is optional, nor to bind every person with every particular of Jeremiah's day.

debates.question: Is the 'deceitful heart' of 17:9 a statement about every human being?

views.label: Yes, a universal diagnosis
views.case: The verse says the heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure, and Scripture says elsewhere that the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth, Genesis 8:21, and that no one is righteous, Romans 3:10. Augustine and the Reformers read it as a description of fallen human nature, which is why they spoke of a need for a new birth.

views.label: A description of Judah's covenant-breaking heart
views.case: The setting is a people who have engraved sin on their hearts, 17:1, and a man who 'turns his heart from the LORD,' 17:5. On this reading the verse is aimed at those who trust in flesh and not at the one who trusts the LORD in 17:7, whose heart is not deceived.

views.label: Universal, but not the last word
views.case: The heart is incurable by the heart's own means, but not by God's. Jeremiah himself promises a new heart in 24:7 and 31:33, and the 'who can understand it?' of 17:9 is answered by 'I, the LORD' in 17:10.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the verse does not end in despair. The question 'who can understand it?' is put so that the answer can be 'I, the LORD, search the heart,' and so that the new covenant can be seen as the cure.

debates.question: Does the Sabbath instruction of 17:19-27 bind Christians?

views.label: The Sabbath principle continues, fulfilled in a weekly day of rest
views.case: The Sabbath rests on creation, Exodus 31:16 and 17, and was given as a sign to Israel and as a day of delight, Isaiah 58:13. Many Reformed and other traditions hold that a weekly rest and worship remains, with the first day as the day of Christ's resurrection, even if the specific rules about loads belonged to Judah.

views.label: The Sabbath is a shadow fulfilled in Christ
views.case: Paul says that no one should be judged about a Sabbath, since these are a shadow and the body belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16 and 17. The rest of Hebrews 4:9 is found by those who rest from their own works in Him, so the weekly day is not a Christian obligation.

views.label: A pattern of rest that serves people
views.case: Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, Mark 2:27, and frees a woman bound for eighteen years on the Sabbath, Luke 13:16. The law's purpose is mercy and trust, and the principle persists as a rhythm of rest that may take different forms.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Jeremiah 17 is about who owns the city's time and whether Judah trusted God to provide. The instruction was not meant to be an arbitrary test but an act of trust, which is the continuing point.

debates.question: Are the fishermen and hunters of 16:16 agents of judgment or of restoration?

views.label: Judgment
views.case: Verse 16 begins 'But for now' and is followed by 'My eyes are on all their ways,' verse 17, and a repayment of iniquity, verse 18. Fishermen and hunters are used for capture elsewhere, as in Habakkuk 1:14 and 15. The two images together describe a complete search, from the water to every mountain and cleft, so that no one escapes.

views.label: Restoration, the gathering of the exiles
views.case: Because verse 15 promises a return from the north and all the lands, some read the fishermen and hunters as those who gather the scattered back. Jesus' call to be 'fishers of men,' Matthew 4:19, may then be heard to echo the image, though His use is not the same.

debates.bearing: The immediate context favours judgment, with the sequence 'first' in verse 18 and the promise in verses 14 and 15 placed before it. In either case, the order is the same: judgment comes before the return.

study.originalLanguages:
The removal in 16:5 is the removal of three covenant gifts, shalom, chesed and rachamim, 'My peace, My loving devotion, and My compassion.' The second and third are the pair at the centre of the LORD's self-description in Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.' To take them away is to withdraw the character of God from the people, not only a convenience, and the prohibition on mourning follows from it: if God has removed compassion, human consolation would be a lie. The words for the banned acts are saphad, to lament aloud, and nud, a word of sympathy that is used of Job's friends coming to 'sympathize' with him, Job 2:11.

The explanation in 16:12 repeats Jeremiah's signature phrase, sherirut libbo ra', 'the stubbornness of his evil heart,' which is also at 7:24 and 18:12. In 16:14 and 15 the oath 'As the LORD lives' is the form in which Israel confessed its founding rescue; the passage proposes that the formula itself will be rewritten, with the new deliverance from the north and all the lands taking the old one's place.

The word for 'fishermen' is dayyagim and for 'hunters' tsayyadim, so the verse speaks of professional catchers sent out by God. In 17:1 the sin is engraved on 'tablets,' luchot, the same word as the stone tablets of the law, Exodus 24:12, and the heart's tablet where the law was meant to be written, Proverbs 3:3. Sin has occupied the place intended for instruction.

The heart in 17:9 is 'aqov, deceitful or crooked, a word from the root behind the name Jacob, whose verb Esau uses in 'he has cheated me twice,' Genesis 27:36; see also Hosea 12:3. The heart is a supplanter. In 17:10 God searches the heart, chaqar, and tests the 'mind,' which the BSB footnote says is literally the kidneys, the seat of the deepest feelings. The speaker is 'I, the LORD,' the emphatic ani YHWH, as the answer to 'who?'

In 17:13 'hope of Israel' is miqveh Yisrael, the same phrase as 14:8. Miqveh also means a gathering of water, as in Genesis 1:10, so the verse that follows, 'the fountain of living water,' sets the hope and the water side by side, and the drought of chapter 14 stands behind it. The Hebrew of 17:21 says to 'guard' your lives, hishshameru benaphshotekhem, so the BSB's 'take heed for yourselves' carries the sense that the Sabbath is about survival. The closing threat, an unquenchable fire in the gates to consume the citadels of Jerusalem, borrows Amos 1:14, where the same fire consumed the citadels of Rabbah. Judah is given the sentence once spoken against the nations.

typology.type: The silenced voices of bride and bridegroom, 16:9
typology.fulfillment: The sign takes away the sounds of joy and gladness, and the book says in 7:34, here and in 25:10 that they are removed, and in 33:10 and 11 that they will return. The correspondence is complete in Christ, who is the Bridegroom, Mark 2:19 and 20, and who begins His signs at a wedding, John 2:1. At the end, the marriage supper of the Lamb is announced, Revelation 19:9, while the voice of the bride and bridegroom is heard no more in Babylon, Revelation 18:23. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's sign proclaims a joy that is withdrawn, while the Bridegroom's presence means that joy is not an occasion but a person.

typology.type: The tree planted by the waters, 17:7 and 8
typology.fulfillment: The blessed man is a tree that does not fear heat or worry in drought and does not stop bearing fruit. The same picture opens the Psalter, Psalm 1:3, and Jesus expresses it as union: 'I am the vine and you are the branches,' John 15:5. The first fulfilment is in Christ Himself, the one who trusted perfectly, and the second in those who remain in Him. The correspondence is real, but it does not mean that any believer is automatically fruitful in drought; the tree is a promise of what it means to be rooted, not an escape from the dry year.

God promises a deliverance that will outshine the exodus from Egypt, so that Israel will swear by the gathering from the north. Isaiah announces that God will make a way in the wilderness, Isaiah 43:18 and 19. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His 'departure,' the Greek word exodos, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, and John says He died to gather the scattered children of God into one, John 11:52. The type is not exhausted, since the final gathering is still ahead, and the old exodus is not discarded but is remembered in a larger frame.

typology.type: The Sabbath as a sign of covenant rest, 17:21 to 27
typology.fulfillment: The Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel, Exodus 31:13, and the city's future turns on it. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, Matthew 12:8, and invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28. Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains, Hebrews 4:9, and Paul calls the day a shadow whose substance is Christ, Colossians 2:16 and 17. The type is fulfilled in that the sign points to a rest that Christ gives. It is limited in that Judah's Sabbath could not give the rest it pointed to.

study.christ:
Jeremiah 17 gives the diagnosis for which the gospel is the answer. The heart is 'beyond cure,' and no human strength reaches it. Jesus agrees: evil thoughts come from within, from the hearts of men, Mark 7:21, and He did not entrust Himself to people because He knew what was in a man, John 2:24 and 25. He also claims the prerogative of 17:10. 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts,' He says in Revelation 2:23, using the LORD's own words in Jeremiah, and He adds that He will repay each according to deeds. The one who knows what is in the heart is the one who has come to deal with it.

The cure is announced in the language of Jeremiah's own book. At the table He says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, and the writer to the Hebrews cites Jeremiah's words about laws written on the heart as fulfilled, Hebrews 8:10. What sin engraved with an iron stylus, the Spirit rewrites, 2 Corinthians 3:3.

Christ is also the true 'blessed man' of 17:7 and 8, who trusted in the LORD when mockers said, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now,' Matthew 27:43. And He is the one who took the 'cursed' of 17:5 onto Himself. Paul says that Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,' so that the blessing might come to the nations, Galatians 3:13 and 14. The man who trusts in mankind is cursed; the One who trusted God was made a curse, so that those who trust Him might be blessed.

He is the 'hope of Israel,' the phrase of 17:13. Paul is in chains 'because of the hope of Israel,' Acts 28:20, and writes of 'Christ Jesus our hope,' 1 Timothy 1:1. And He is the fountain of living water that the unfaithful forsook, 17:13: He offers living water to the woman at the well, John 4:10, and calls the thirsty to come to Him, John 7:37 and 38.

On the Sabbath, Jesus heals, frees and tells a healed man to pick up his mat and walk, John 5:8 to 10, which brought the charge that it was unlawful to carry it. The link to Jeremiah's 'do not carry a load' is the way the leaders applied the rule, not a statement that Jesus broke Jeremiah's command, and the whole incident shows Him as the Lord of the day.

A caution: Jeremiah is not Jesus, and not every image here is a coded picture of Him. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of Jeremiah's promises, and on the fit between a diagnosis and a Physician.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who knows the heart. The man who cannot understand his own heart, 17:9, is fully known by the LORD who searches it and examines it, 17:10. This is the doctrine of divine omniscience in a form that is neither detached nor abstract: God judges 'a man according to his way,' not by a distant standard but by what is actually in him. The verse at the same time sets up the tension that runs through Scripture, that God rewards according to deeds and that the human heart cannot be trusted to produce them. The tension is held by the new covenant, where God writes what He demands.

He is the God who owns His land. 'My land' and 'My inheritance' in 16:18 explain why defilement by idols brings expulsion. He is not a tribal deity who can be moved by offerings; He is the owner, and a dwelling with Him requires a clean place.

He is the God of the exodus and the God who will exceed it. The promise in 16:14 and 15 means that His identity is not tied to a single act. He rescued once, and He will rescue again on a larger scale, which is the shape of His faithfulness throughout the book.

He is just in the sense that every sentence has a reason. The question 'What is our guilt?' in 16:10 is answered with a clear reply. Even the severe 'I will show you no favor' in 16:13 is followed by the offer of a return. His patience is shown even at the end, where the Sabbath sermon in 17:19 to 27 sets out a conditional promise of David's throne, a populated city and worshipers from all around. The offer is real, and the threat of an unquenchable fire is real.

He is a refuge in distress, 16:19 and 17:17. The prophet who is forbidden every comfort calls God 'my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress.' The God who strips away consolation is the one in whom consolation is found.

He is the God of the nations. 16:19 to 21 foresees the nations coming from the ends of the earth and saying their fathers inherited nothing but lies. The God of Israel is not a local power. His purpose in judgment includes making His power and might known, so that they will know that His name is the LORD, 16:21.

For worship, this means that confession and trust belong together. We admit that we cannot read our own hearts, and we put our trust in the One who can. We also receive the Sabbath not as a burden but as a weekly act of believing that He provides.

crossReferences.note: The man who delights in the law is like a tree planted by streams of water whose leaf does not wither. Jeremiah 17:7 and 8 uses nearly the same picture but sets it against the shrub of verse 6, making it a choice of trust. The psalm begins with delight in God's word, while Jeremiah begins with trust in God Himself.

The answer to the deceitful heart of 17:9. God promises a covenant in which the law is written on the heart. The iron stylus of 17:1 engraved sin; in the new covenant God Himself writes what He requires, and every person knows Him.

Paul says the Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit on tablets of human hearts. The vocabulary of tablets and hearts takes up Jeremiah 17:1 and 31:33, and shows the church as the place where the engraving is replaced.

The first statement of the charge: the people forsook the fountain of living water and dug broken cisterns. Jeremiah 17:13 returns to it, so the chapters from 2 to 17 form a long argument about where water is to be found.

The promise of 16:14 and 15 repeats almost word for word, with the new deliverance replacing the oath by the exodus. The doublet shows that the promise of return was not a passing comfort but a settled part of Jeremiah's message.

Ezekiel's wife dies and he is told not to mourn, so that the people may understand that their own loss will be beyond mourning. It is the closest parallel to Jeremiah 16:5 to 9, and shows that sign acts of forbidden grief were part of the prophets' work.

The voice of the bride and bridegroom will never be heard again in Babylon. John takes the language of Jeremiah 7:34 and 16:9 and applies it to the final enemy city, so that the silence that fell on Jerusalem returns on the power that opposed God's people.

Nehemiah finds Sabbath trade at the gates of Jerusalem and reminds the nobles that such behaviour brought disaster on their fathers. It shows the sermon of Jeremiah 17:19 to 27 as a standing memory, and that the issue the prophet raised had returned.

The LORD kindles a fire in the walls of Rabbah to consume its citadels. Jeremiah 17:27 uses the same formula for Jerusalem, so that the city that had listened to oracles against the nations hears one against itself.
Jesus says that He is the One who searches minds and hearts and will repay each according to deeds. The words belong to the LORD in Jeremiah 17:10, and here the risen Christ uses them of Himself.

Jesus tells a healed man to pick up his mat and walk on the Sabbath, and the leaders object that it is unlawful to carry it. The scene reads the carrying of loads, which Jeremiah 17:21 forbade, in the light of Jesus' authority over the day.

Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, so that the blessing might come to the nations. Jeremiah 17:5 to 8 sets curse and blessing side by side, and Paul shows how the one who bore the curse gives the blessing.

study.oneStory:
Genesis shows the heart going wrong. After the flood God says that the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth, Genesis 8:21, and the prophets will not say otherwise. Jeremiah 17:9 gathers that long observation into a single verse and then asks the question left over from Eden: if the heart is beyond cure, what can be done? The rest of the Bible is the answer.

The first stage of the answer is the covenant at Sinai, where the law is written on stone tablets, and the failure of that stage is described here, with sin engraved on tablets of the heart. The prophets then promise a different writing. Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 foresee a new heart, and in the upper room Jesus says the cup is the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20. Pentecost and the gift of the Spirit begin it, and the church becomes a letter written by the Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:3.

The chapter also touches the story of rest. God rested on the seventh day, Exodus 31:17, and gave Israel the Sabbath as a sign. Judah's failure to keep it is one of the reasons the land ends up desolate, and in the end the land does enjoy its Sabbaths for seventy years in the exile, 2 Chronicles 36:21. Jesus invites the weary to rest, Matthew 11:28, and Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, Hebrews 4:9.

The thread of exile and return runs through 16:14 and 15. God's people are scattered, and the story promises a return that surpasses the first exodus. The return begins with a remnant from Babylon, deepens with the gathering in Christ, John 11:52, and ends in the new creation. In Revelation the nations come bringing their glory, Revelation 21:24 to 26, which is what Jeremiah 16:19 foresaw, and the tree of life on either side of the river has leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The throne of God and of the Lamb is there, Revelation 22:3, and the 'glorious throne, exalted from the beginning' of Jeremiah 17:12 is no longer a hope but a home. The man who trusts the LORD finds that he is the tree planted by the river.

quiz.q: What three ordinary life events is Jeremiah forbidden from participating in, as a sign act?

options.text: Marriage, mourning for the dead, and feasting with others.
options.note: Verses 16:2, 5, and 8 forbid each of these in turn.

options.text: Traveling, teaching, and prophesying.
options.note: This contradicts Jeremiah's actual, ongoing prophetic ministry throughout the book.

options.text: Prayer, fasting, and temple worship.
options.note: These are not what is forbidden; the passage concerns Jeremiah's social and family life, not his acts of worship.

options.text: Farming, trading, and building.
options.note: These economic activities are not the specific things forbidden in this passage.

quiz.q: According to 16:14-15, what future event will eventually replace the exodus from Egypt as Israel's defining oath?

options.text: The LORD bringing the Israelites back from the land of the north and all the other lands where He had banished them.
options.note: Verses 14-15 state this future hope directly.

options.text: The end of all covenant relationship between God and Israel.
options.note: This contradicts the hopeful restoration promised in these verses.

options.text: The rebuilding of Solomon's original temple.
options.note: Temple rebuilding is not the specific future event named in these verses.

options.text: The defeat of Babylon by a foreign army.
options.note: The focus of these verses is on Israel's own restoration and gathering, not a specific foreign military defeat.

quiz.q: What does 17:9 say about the human heart?

options.text: It is deceitful above all things and beyond cure; no one can fully understand it.
options.note: Verse 9 states this directly and starkly.

options.text: It is fully trustworthy for guiding right decisions.
options.note: This directly contradicts the verse's stark assessment of the heart.

options.text: It only becomes corrupt in old age.
options.note: The deceitfulness described is not tied to age anywhere in the text.

options.text: It is basically good and only occasionally misled.
options.note: This softens the verse's actual, much starker claim about the heart's deceitfulness.

quiz.q: What image is used for the person who trusts in the LORD in 17:7-8?

options.text: A tree planted by the waters, whose leaves stay green and which never stops bearing fruit even in drought.
options.note: Verse 8 uses exactly this image.

options.text: A shrub in the parched places of the desert.
options.note: This image is actually used for the cursed person who trusts in man, verse 6, the opposite of the blessed person's image.

options.text: A lamp that never runs out of oil.
options.note: This is not the image used in these verses.

options.text: A bird flying swiftly to escape a coming storm.
options.note: This is not the image used for trust in the LORD in this passage.

quiz.q: What does God command regarding the Sabbath in 17:21-22?

options.text: Not to carry any load or do any work on the Sabbath day, but to keep it holy.
options.note: Verses 21-22 state this command plainly.

options.text: To abolish the Sabbath entirely as no longer necessary.
options.note: This directly contradicts the command to keep the Sabbath holy.

options.text: To fast completely from food on the Sabbath day.
options.note: Fasting is not mentioned as part of this specific Sabbath command.

options.text: To offer double sacrifices on the Sabbath day.
options.note: This is not the specific command given; the focus is on refraining from carrying loads and doing work.

questions: Jeremiah was forbidden even the ordinary joys of marriage, mourning, and feasting as a sign of coming judgment. Has God ever asked you to give up something good for the sake of a larger, harder calling?
God promises a future so great it will eclipse the memory of the exodus itself. What present difficulty makes it hard for you to believe God has a greater future planned?
Jeremiah says the heart is deceitful above all things. Where have you trusted your own heart's judgment more than you should have?
The blessed person is like a tree planted by the waters, unaffected by drought. What would it look like practically for you to plant your roots more deeply in trusting God this week?
God calls Judah to keep the Sabbath holy as a test of covenant loyalty. What regular rhythm of rest or worship might God be calling you to guard more carefully?

translationNotes.note: The house of mourning likely refers to a formal mourning custom or gathering in the ancient Near East, not merely private grief, making Jeremiah's exclusion from it a publicly visible sign.
The image of sin written with an iron stylus and a diamond point emphasizes permanence, sin engraved rather than easily erased, on both the heart and the altars themselves.

The Hebrew word rendered deceitful shares a root with the name Jacob, possibly echoing Jacob's own history of deception, Genesis 27, and reinforcing that this is a universal human condition, not a fault unique to Judah's generation.
